title: Unveiling Privacy, Memorization, and Input Curvature Links

en.text: When we train a deep neural network, we want it to learn patterns, not to file away individual training examples verbatim. Yet a large body of work shows that deep networks do memorize part of their training data, especially the rare, hard, and noisy examples. That memorization is entangled with generalization and noisy learning, and it is also a privacy problem: if a model has memorized someone's data, an attacker may be able to pull it back out.

The trouble is measuring which examples a model has actually memorized. Feldman's stability-based memorization score gives a rigorous definition, but it is brutally expensive: scoring a single example means training hundreds or thousands of models on datasets that do and do not contain it. So researchers went looking for a cheaper stand-in, and the most promising one is input loss curvature, the trace of the Hessian of the loss with respect to the input. It costs roughly three orders of magnitude less to compute than the memorization score.

Until now, using curvature as a proxy for memorization was purely empirical. The two quantities rose and fell together in experiments, but nobody could say why, and nobody knew how either related to differential privacy. This paper, from Purdue University and presented at ICML 2024, supplies the missing theory. It ties memorization, input loss curvature, and differential privacy together with a set of rigorous upper bounds that close into a triangle.

en.caption: Figure 1. The paper's framework. Theorem 5.1 bounds memorization by input loss curvature, Theorem 5.3 bounds average curvature by the differential-privacy parameter, and Theorem 5.4 chains the two to bound memorization directly by privacy. The three edges close into a triangle.

en.text: Paper and code: the arXiv paper is at https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18726 .
Why a cheap proxy still needs a theory

The usual tool for counterfactual questions in deep learning, the kind that ask what happens if we remove one example, is the influence function. But influence functions lean on a strong assumption: that the loss Hessian is convex and positive-definite. For real deep networks, that condition essentially never holds. Input loss curvature, by contrast, only needs a second-order expansion of the loss and makes no assumption about Hessian convexity or definiteness, which makes it a better fit for analyzing deep networks.

But cheap and convenient is not the same as correct. Without a proof that curvature actually controls memorization, swapping in curvature for the memorization score is just a lucky empirical habit. The question the paper sets out to answer is exactly this: can the link between curvature and memorization be written as a checkable mathematical bound?
What curvature is actually measuring

Before the theory, it helps to build some intuition. If you rank the training set by input loss curvature, a clean stratification appears. Low-curvature examples are prototypical members of their class, while high-curvature examples are the rare, difficult, more-likely-memorized outliers. That is precisely the behavior the memorization score captures, and it is the intuitive reason curvature can serve as a proxy at all.

en.caption: Figure 2. ImageNet training images ranked by input loss curvature from a single ResNet18, one class per row. The ten left columns are the lowest-curvature samples, canonical in pose and background; the ten right columns are the highest-curvature samples, with unusual framing and clutter that look more like memorized instances.

en.text: Three bounds, one for each edge of the triangle

The theory starts from a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, using the Nesterov-Polyak bound to bring in the input Hessian. The key move is to choose a zero-mean perturbation so that the first-order terms vanish under expectation, leaving an upper bound on memorization written in terms of input loss curvature plus a data-independent constant that bundles up stability, generalization, and model-bias terms. That is Theorem 5.1: curvature controls memorization.

A parallel derivation, combined with the definition of differential privacy, yields a new result, Theorem 5.3: a stronger privacy guarantee, meaning a smaller privacy budget ε, forces lower average input loss curvature. Chain the two edges and you get Theorem 5.4, which bounds memorization directly by privacy. None of these steps assumes Hessian convexity or positive-definiteness, so the results carry over directly to the deep networks we actually train.

To make curvature practical to measure, the authors estimate the trace of the Hessian with Hutchinson's trace estimator, configured with a finite-difference step of h = 1e-3 and n = 10 Rademacher probe vectors, sidestepping any need to form the full Hessian.
Edge one: memorization rises linearly with curvature

A theory has to earn its keep on real data. The authors reuse Feldman & Zhang's (2020) precomputed memorization scores and released model ensembles: 1000 Small Inception models on CIFAR100 and 100 ResNet50 models on ImageNet, averaging each example's memorization score and curvature across the ensemble.

en.caption: Figure 4. At the end of training on CIFAR100, average memorization score (x-axis) against average curvature score (y-axis), averaged over 1000 Small Inception models. Blue crosses are empirical data, the red dashed line is the theory best fit, and the green dashed line is the sub-population bound. The points hug the predicted curve, confirming Theorem 5.1.

en.text: The scatter tracks the predicted curve almost exactly: the higher an example's memorization score, the larger its input loss curvature, in a clean, monotone, near-linear relationship. The paper notes the trend is especially crisp on ImageNet. This suggests curvature is not merely correlated with memorization by accident, but bounds it in the way the theorem predicts.
Edge two: stronger privacy pushes curvature down

For the privacy edge, the authors train ResNet18 with DP-SGD, sweeping the privacy budget ε over 1, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 at a fixed δ = 1e-5, averaging over 10 random seeds per budget, and measuring the resulting input loss curvature.

en.caption: Figure 7. Privacy budget (x-axis, smaller means stronger privacy) against input loss curvature (y-axis) for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. The dashed best-fit curve is the shape predicted by Theorem 5.3, and the empirical points land on it: a tighter budget yields lower curvature.

en.text: As the privacy budget tightens (smaller ε), input loss curvature falls, and the shape of that decline matches the best-fit curve the theory predicts. In other words, the differential-privacy mechanism drives input loss curvature down along exactly the trajectory Theorem 5.3 predicts.
Edge three: privacy caps memorization

The last edge connects privacy and memorization directly. On CIFAR100, the authors watch how memorization scores move with the budget once differential privacy is applied, and compare against the upper bound Theorem 5.4 provides.

en.caption: Figure 8. Differential-privacy budget (x-axis) against memorization (y-axis, log scale) on CIFAR100. Blue crosses are empirical memorization scores; the red dashed line is the Theorem 5.4 upper bound. The empirical values stay far below the bound, showing privacy really does cap memorization.

en.text: As the budget loosens, the memorization of the affected examples, particularly the most-memorized ones, rises as expected, but stays comfortably beneath the theoretical bound throughout. With that, all three edges close: curvature bounds memorization, privacy bounds curvature, and so privacy bounds memorization too.
The numbers at a glance

en.caption: Table 1. Key settings and numbers from the paper.
rows: Hutchinson trace, h = 1e-3, n = 10 Rademacher vectors

en.text: Why it matters, and where it stops

The contribution is that a relationship which used to be an empirical coincidence, curvature standing in for memorization, now rests on firm theory. Curvature is provably an upper bound on memorization, curvature is itself capped by the differential-privacy parameter, and so privacy bounds memorization as well. Because the framework needs no Hessian-convexity assumptions, it applies directly to real deep networks, and its predictions hold up on CIFAR and ImageNet.

For a practitioner, the most immediate payoff is a screening tool. Because high-curvature examples are the rare, hard, likely-memorized ones (Figure 2), and curvature is cheap to compute, a single trained model plus Hutchinson's estimator can surface the training points most at risk of being memorized, without the thousand-model ensemble Feldman's score demands. The theory is what licenses reading curvature this way, rather than treating the alignment as a lucky correlation.

The privacy edge adds a second lever. Since a tighter privacy budget provably lowers both curvature and memorization, curvature also becomes a cheap diagnostic for how much a differentially private training run is actually suppressing memorization, a quantity that is otherwise expensive to audit directly.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly: these are upper-bound results resting on assumptions of error stability, generalization, model bias, and dataset adjacency, together with bounded loss, and the experiments center on image classification with standard vision architectures. Still, the practical message is clear. Using cheap curvature in place of expensive memorization scores now has a theoretical license, and privacy mechanisms reduce leakage precisely because they provably drive down both curvature and memorization at once.

zh.text: 训练一个深度神经网络时，我们通常希望它学到的是“规律”，而不是把某些训练样本原封不动地背下来。但大量研究已经发现，深度网络确实会记住（memorize）一部分训练数据，尤其是那些罕见、困难、带噪声的样本。这种“记忆化”既和泛化、噪声学习有关，也直接关系到隐私：如果一个模型把某个人的数据背了下来，攻击者就有可能把它还原出来。

问题在于，怎么量化“一个模型到底记住了哪些样本”。Feldman 提出的基于稳定性的记忆化分数（memorization score）给出了严谨的定义，但代价极高：要估计单个样本的分数，需要在“包含该样本”和“不包含该样本”的数据集上反复训练成百上千个模型。于是研究者开始寻找便宜的替代指标，其中最有希望的是输入损失曲率（input loss curvature），也就是损失对输入的 Hessian 矩阵的迹（trace）。它的计算成本大约只有记忆化分数的千分之一。
此前，曲率能作为记忆化的代理，纯粹是经验观察：两者在实验里同涨同落，但没人说得清为什么，更没人知道它们和差分隐私（differential privacy）之间是什么关系。这篇来自 Purdue University、发表于 ICML 2024 的论文补上了缺失的理论，把记忆化、输入损失曲率、差分隐私三者用一组严格的上界连成了一个三角形。

zh.caption: 图1 论文的核心框架：Theorem 5.1 证明输入损失曲率是记忆化的上界，Theorem 5.3 证明差分隐私参数是平均曲率的上界，Theorem 5.4 则把两者串起来，用隐私直接约束记忆化。三条边构成一个闭合三角形。

zh.text: 论文与代码：arXiv 论文见 https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18726 。
为什么“便宜的代理”需要一个理论
在深度学习里，研究“去掉某个样本会发生什么”这类反事实（counterfactual）问题，常用的工具是影响函数（influence function）。但影响函数依赖一个强假设：损失的 Hessian 是凸的、正定的。对真实的深度网络来说，这个条件几乎不成立。相比之下，输入损失曲率只需要对损失做一次二阶展开，不需要任何关于 Hessian 凸性或正定性的假设，因此更适合分析深度网络。
但“便宜”和“好用”不等于“正确”。如果不能证明曲率确实约束了记忆化，那么用曲率替代记忆化分数就只是一种碰运气的经验做法。这篇论文要回答的正是这个问题：曲率和记忆化之间的联系，能不能被写成一个可以验证的数学上界？
曲率到底在衡量什么
在深入理论之前，先建立一点直觉。如果对训练集里的样本按输入损失曲率排序，会看到一个很清晰的分层：曲率低的样本是该类别的“典型代表”，曲率高的样本则是罕见、困难、更可能被模型死记硬背的个例。这与记忆化分数所刻画的现象高度一致，正是曲率能作为代理的直观来源。

zh.caption: 图2 用单个 ResNet18 在 ImageNet 上计算的输入损失曲率对训练样本排序，每行是一个类别。左侧十列是曲率最低的样本，姿态、背景都很“标准”；右侧十列是曲率最高的样本，构图罕见、遮挡多、更接近被记住的个例。

zh.text: 三条上界：把三角形的每条边都证出来
论文的理论从损失的二阶泰勒展开出发，借助 Nesterov-Polyak 上界引入输入 Hessian。关键技巧是选取一个零均值的扰动，使一阶项在取期望后消失，剩下的正是用输入损失曲率表示的记忆化上界，外加一个与数据无关的常数项（它把稳定性、泛化、模型偏置等因素打包在一起）。这就是 Theorem 5.1：记忆化被曲率控制。
沿着类似的思路，再结合差分隐私的定义，可以证明一条全新的结果（Theorem 5.3）：更强的隐私保护（即更小的隐私预算 ε）会强制降低平均输入损失曲率。把这两条边接起来，就得到 Theorem 5.4：隐私直接给出了记忆化的上界。整套推导不需要任何 Hessian 凸性或正定性假设，因此可以直接套用到真实的深度网络上。
为了让曲率真正可算，作者用 Hutchinson 迹估计器（Hutchinson's trace estimator）来近似 Hessian 的迹，配置为有限差分步长 h = 1e-3、n = 10 个 Rademacher 探测向量，避免了显式计算整个 Hessian。
第一条边：记忆化随曲率线性上升
理论要落地，就得在真实数据上验证。作者直接使用 Feldman & Zhang (2020) 预计算的记忆化分数和他们公开的模型集合：CIFAR100 上 1000 个 Small Inception，ImageNet 上 100 个 ResNet50，把每个样本的记忆化分数和曲率在这些模型上取平均。

zh.caption: 图4 训练结束时，CIFAR100 上平均记忆化分数（横轴）与平均曲率分数（纵轴）的关系（1000 个 Small Inception 模型平均）。蓝色叉是经验数据，红色虚线是理论最佳拟合，绿色虚线是子群（sub-population）上界。经验点紧贴理论曲线，验证了 Theorem 5.1。

zh.text: 散点几乎沿着理论预测的曲线排列：记忆化分数越高，输入损失曲率越大，二者呈现清晰的单调、近线性关系。论文指出这一趋势在 ImageNet 上尤其干净。这说明曲率不只是“碰巧相关”，而是按理论预测的方式约束着记忆化。
第二条边：更强的隐私压低曲率
对于隐私这条边，作者用 DP-SGD 训练 ResNet18，把隐私预算 ε 在 1、10、20、30、40、50 之间扫描（固定 δ = 1e-5），每个预算下对 10 个随机种子取平均，再测量对应的输入损失曲率。

zh.caption: 图7 隐私预算（横轴，越小隐私越强）与输入损失曲率（纵轴）的关系，CIFAR10 与 CIFAR100。虚线是 Theorem 5.3 预测的最佳拟合曲线，经验点落在其上：预算越小，曲率越低。

zh.text: 当隐私预算收紧（ε 变小）时，输入损失曲率随之下降，且下降的形状与理论预测的最佳拟合曲线一致。换句话说，差分隐私机制确实在按理论刻画的方式压低曲率，这正是 Theorem 5.3 想说的。
第三条边：隐私为记忆化封顶
最后一条边把隐私和记忆化直接连起来。在 CIFAR100 上，作者观察加了差分隐私之后记忆化分数如何随预算变化，并与 Theorem 5.4 给出的理论上界对照。

zh.caption: 图8 CIFAR100 上差分隐私预算（横轴）与记忆化（纵轴，对数刻度）的关系。蓝色叉是经验记忆化分数，红色虚线是 Theorem 5.4 的理论上界。经验值始终远低于上界，说明隐私确实为记忆化封了顶。

zh.text: 随着预算放宽，被记住的样本（尤其是最容易被记住的那批）记忆化分数如预期上升，但始终稳稳待在理论上界之下。三条边至此全部闭合：曲率约束记忆化，隐私约束曲率，隐私因此也约束记忆化。
关键数字一览

zh.caption: 表1 论文的关键设定与数字
rows: 曲率相对记忆化分数的计算成本
CIFAR100：1000 个 Small Inception；ImageNet：100 个 ResNet50
隐私预算 ε 扫描
Hutchinson 迹估计，h = 1e-3，n = 10 个 Rademacher 向量

zh.text: 意义与边界
这项工作的价值在于：过去只是经验巧合的“曲率约等于记忆化”，现在有了严格的理论支撑。曲率被证明是记忆化的上界，而曲率本身又被差分隐私参数封顶，于是隐私也约束了记忆化。因为整套框架不依赖 Hessian 凸性假设，它可以直接用于真实的深度网络，其预测也在 CIFAR 和 ImageNet 上得到了验证。
对实践者来说，最直接的收益是一个筛查工具。既然高曲率样本正是那些罕见、困难、更可能被记住的样本（见图2），而曲率的计算又很便宜，那么只需一个训练好的模型加上 Hutchinson 估计器，就能在不训练 Feldman 分数所需的上千个模型的前提下，标记出最可能被记忆化、隐私风险最高的训练样本。正是这套理论，让“把曲率当作记忆化的读数”从一种碰巧相关变成有据可依的做法。
隐私这条边则提供了第二个抓手。既然更紧的隐私预算可以被证明地同时压低曲率和记忆化，那么曲率本身也就成了一个便宜的诊断量：它能间接反映一次差分隐私训练究竟把记忆化压低了多少，而这个量原本很难直接审计。
需要注意边界：这些是上界结果，依赖误差稳定性、泛化、模型偏置、数据集邻接等假设与有界损失条件；实验也集中在图像分类和标准视觉架构上。但对实践者来说，结论足够清晰：用便宜的曲率测量替代昂贵的记忆化分数，如今有了理论许可，而隐私机制之所以能减少泄漏，也因为它可证明地同时压低了曲率和记忆化。

在深度学习里，研究“去掉某个样本会发生什么”这类反事实（counterfactual）问题，常用的工具是影响函数（influence function）。但影响函数依赖一个强假设：损失的 Hessian 是凸的、正定的。对真实的深度网络来说，这个条件几乎不成立。相比之下，输入损失曲率只需要对损失做一次二阶展开，不需要任何关于 Hessian 凸性或正定性的假设，因此更适合分析深度网络。
但“便宜”和“好用”不等于“正确”。如果不能证明曲率确实约束了记忆化，那么用曲率替代记忆化分数就只是一种碰运气的经验做法。这篇论文要回答的正是这个问题：曲率和记忆化之间的联系，能不能被写成一个可以验证的数学上界？

en.caption: Figure 1. The paper's framework. Theorem 5.1 bounds memorization by input loss curvature, Theorem 5.3 bounds average curvature by the differential-privacy parameter, and Theorem 5.4 chains the two to bound memorization directly by privacy. The three edges close into a triangle.

en.text: Why it matters, and where it stops

The contribution is that a relationship which used to be an empirical coincidence, curvature standing in for memorization, now rests on firm theory. Curvature is provably an upper bound on memorization, curvature is itself capped by the differential-privacy parameter, and so privacy bounds memorization as well. Because the framework needs no Hessian-convexity assumptions, it applies directly to real deep networks, and its predictions hold up on CIFAR and ImageNet.

For a practitioner, the most immediate payoff is a screening tool. Because high-curvature examples are the rare, hard, likely-memorized ones (Figure 2), and curvature is cheap to compute, a single trained model plus Hutchinson's estimator can surface the training points most at risk of being memorized, without the thousand-model ensemble Feldman's score demands. The theory is what licenses reading curvature this way, rather than treating the alignment as a lucky correlation.

The privacy edge adds a second lever. Since a tighter privacy budget provably lowers both curvature and memorization, curvature also becomes a cheap diagnostic for how much a differentially private training run is actually suppressing memorization, a quantity that is otherwise expensive to audit directly.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly: these are upper-bound results resting on assumptions of error stability, generalization, model bias, and dataset adjacency, together with bounded loss, and the experiments center on image classification with standard vision architectures. Still, the practical message is clear. Using cheap curvature in place of expensive memorization scores now has a theoretical license, and privacy mechanisms reduce leakage precisely because they provably drive down both curvature and memorization at once.

zh.text: 训练一个深度神经网络时，我们通常希望它学到的是“规律”，而不是把某些训练样本原封不动地背下来。但大量研究已经发现，深度网络确实会记住（memorize）一部分训练数据，尤其是那些罕见、困难、带噪声的样本。这种“记忆化”既和泛化、噪声学习有关，也直接关系到隐私：如果一个模型把某个人的数据背了下来，攻击者就有可能把它还原出来。

问题在于，怎么量化“一个模型到底记住了哪些样本”。Feldman 提出的基于稳定性的记忆化分数（memorization score）给出了严谨的定义，但代价极高：要估计单个样本的分数，需要在“包含该样本”和“不包含该样本”的数据集上反复训练成百上千个模型。于是研究者开始寻找便宜的替代指标，其中最有希望的是输入损失曲率（input loss curvature），也就是损失对输入的 Hessian 矩阵的迹（trace）。它的计算成本大约只有记忆化分数的千分之一。
此前，曲率能作为记忆化的代理，纯粹是经验观察：两者在实验里同涨同落，但没人说得清为什么，更没人知道它们和差分隐私（differential privacy）之间是什么关系。这篇来自 Purdue University、发表于 ICML 2024 的论文补上了缺失的理论，把记忆化、输入损失曲率、差分隐私三者用一组严格的上界连成了一个三角形。

en.caption: Figure 1. The paper's framework. Theorem 5.1 bounds memorization by input loss curvature, Theorem 5.3 bounds average curvature by the differential-privacy parameter, and Theorem 5.4 chains the two to bound memorization directly by privacy. The three edges close into a triangle.

en.text: Three bounds, one for each edge of the triangle

The theory starts from a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, using the Nesterov-Polyak bound to bring in the input Hessian. The key move is to choose a zero-mean perturbation so that the first-order terms vanish under expectation, leaving an upper bound on memorization written in terms of input loss curvature plus a data-independent constant that bundles up stability, generalization, and model-bias terms. That is Theorem 5.1: curvature controls memorization.

A parallel derivation, combined with the definition of differential privacy, yields a new result, Theorem 5.3: a stronger privacy guarantee, meaning a smaller privacy budget ε, forces lower average input loss curvature. Chain the two edges and you get Theorem 5.4, which bounds memorization directly by privacy. None of these steps assumes Hessian convexity or positive-definiteness, so the results carry over directly to the deep networks we actually train.

To make curvature practical to measure, the authors estimate the trace of the Hessian with Hutchinson's trace estimator, configured with a finite-difference step of h = 1e-3 and n = 10 Rademacher probe vectors, sidestepping any need to form the full Hessian.

en.text: When we train a deep neural network, we want it to learn patterns, not to file away individual training examples verbatim. Yet a large body of work shows that deep networks do memorize part of their training data, especially the rare, hard, and noisy examples. That memorization is entangled with generalization and noisy learning, and it is also a privacy problem: if a model has memorized someone's data, an attacker may be able to pull it back out.

The trouble is measuring which examples a model has actually memorized. Feldman's stability-based memorization score gives a rigorous definition, but it is brutally expensive: scoring a single example means training hundreds or thousands of models on datasets that do and do not contain it. It costs roughly three orders of magnitude less to compute than the memorization score.

Until now, using curvature as a proxy for memorization was purely empirical. The two quantities rose and fell together in experiments, but nobody could say why, and nobody knew how either related to differential privacy. This paper, from Purdue University and presented at ICML 2024, supplies the missing theory. It ties memorization, input loss curvature, and differential privacy together with a set of rigorous upper bounds that close into a triangle.

For the privacy edge, the authors train ResNet18 with DP-SGD, sweeping the privacy budget ε over 1, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 at a fixed δ = 1e-5, averaging over 10 random seeds per budget, and measuring the resulting input loss curvature.

Because high-curvature examples are the rare, hard, likely-memorized ones (Figure 2), and curvature is cheap to compute, a single trained model plus Hutchinson's estimator can surface the training points most at risk of being memorized, without the thousand-model ensemble Feldman's score demands. The theory is what licenses reading curvature this way, rather than treating the alignment as a lucky correlation.

The privacy edge adds a second lever. Since a tighter privacy budget provably lowers both curvature and memorization, curvature also becomes a cheap diagnostic for how much a differentially private training run is actually suppressing memorization, a quantity that is otherwise expensive to audit directly.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly: these are upper-bound results resting on assumptions of error stability, generalization, model bias, and dataset adjacency, together with bounded loss, and the experiments center on image classification with standard vision architectures. Still, the practical message is clear. Using cheap curvature in place of expensive memorization scores now has a theoretical license, and privacy mechanisms reduce leakage precisely because they provably drive down both curvature and memorization at once.

zh.caption: 图1 论文的核心框架：Theorem 5.1 证明输入损失曲率是记忆化的上界，Theorem 5.3 证明差分隐私参数是平均曲率的上界，Theorem 5.4 则把两者串起来，用隐私直接约束记忆化。三条边构成一个闭合三角形。

zh.text: 意义与边界
这项工作的价值在于：过去只是经验巧合的“曲率约等于记忆化”，现在有了严格的理论支撑。曲率被证明是记忆化的上界，而曲率本身又被差分隐私参数封顶，于是隐私也约束了记忆化。因为整套框架不依赖 Hessian 凸性假设，它可以直接用于真实的深度网络，其预测也在 CIFAR 和 ImageNet 上得到了验证。
对实践者来说，最直接的收益是一个筛查工具。既然高曲率样本正是那些罕见、困难、更可能被记住的样本（见图2），而曲率的计算又很便宜，那么只需一个训练好的模型加上 Hutchinson 估计器，就能在不训练 Feldman 分数所需的上千个模型的前提下，标记出最可能被记忆化、隐私风险最高的训练样本。正是这套理论，让“把曲率当作记忆化的读数”从一种碰巧相关变成有据可依的做法。
隐私这条边则提供了第二个抓手。既然更紧的隐私预算可以被证明地同时压低曲率和记忆化，那么曲率本身也就成了一个便宜的诊断量：它能间接反映一次差分隐私训练究竟把记忆化压低了多少，而这个量原本很难直接审计。
需要注意边界：这些是上界结果，依赖误差稳定性、泛化、模型偏置、数据集邻接等假设与有界损失条件；实验也集中在图像分类和标准视觉架构上。但对实践者来说，结论足够清晰：用便宜的曲率测量替代昂贵的记忆化分数，如今有了理论许可，而隐私机制之所以能减少泄漏，也因为它可证明地同时压低了曲率和记忆化。
